title: Phase 11b: three-way differential suite (ours, btc-verified, Core) with wtxid, regression set, campaign and negative control
description:
## Outcome
A three-way differential test suite gives the same transaction bytes to this repo's `bitcoin` package, to btc-verified @ `2fdeb40` (through our upgraded copy), and to Bitcoin Core, and compares what each observably does. It runs in the second CI job (the owner's answer to plan §7 question 3), with zero unexplained disagreements and a working negative control. `bitcoin` gains `Transaction.wtxid`.

## Why this exists
Plan.md §7, deliverable 11b. The external analysis asks for differential testing first, following the method of btc-verified's October update ("btc-verified October update: connecting map to territory", Delving Bitcoin, 2026-10-19, https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/btc-verified-october-update-connecting-map-to-territory/2964). btc-verified implements that method in `Fuzz/` and `Kernel/` @ `2fdeb40` (see `Fuzz/README.md`):
- the same bytes go to each implementation;
- observable behaviour is compared;
- fixed regression inputs, including size boundaries, are replayed on every run;
- a seeded campaign runs with a recorded budget;
- an injected-disagreement negative control proves the detector works;
- CI fails on any disagreement.

## Scope
- **`Transaction.wtxid`** in `bitcoin`: SHA-256d of `serializeWitnessTransaction`, in wire order like `txid`. Test it on published vectors (a BIP143/BIP144 SegWit transaction with a known wtxid, plus a legacy one where it equals the txid).
- **The three implementations.** Each runs as its own process and exchanges one hex transaction per line with one JSON observation per line:
  1. *Ours:* `parseTransaction` with `allowWitness` true and false, then `serializeWitnessTransaction`, `txid` and `wtxid` on each accepted value.
  2. *btc-verified:* a small test-only driver that imports `BtcVerified` from our upgraded copy (Phase 11a, 2 of 2: btc-verified @ `2fdeb40` on Lean v4.35.0), pinned by commit, so it builds on this repo's toolchain. That follows from the owner's answer to plan §7 question 1 (2026-10-23). On the witness path it runs the packed `decodeTx`, then `encodeTx`, `Tx.txid` and `Tx.wtxid`. On the non-witness path it runs the packed `TxBody` codec (decode, then encode) and `TxBody.txid`; `TxBody` is the legacy wire form and allows zero inputs (docs/btc-verified-integration.md N17). Nothing from btc-verified is committed. The driver is "MIT OR Apache-2.0" like every other package; our upgraded copy and Mathlib are pinned build-time dependencies, never copied (the owner's answer to plan §7 question 2, 2026-10-23).
  3. *Core*, as **recorded answers** (the owner's answer to plan §7 question 4, 2026-10-23). A committed script, using the plan §6 #4 machinery (a throwaway regtest `bitcoind` from nix in a temp dir, no wallet needed), records Core's answer to `decoderawtransaction <hex> true` and `<hex> false` for every input: the regression set and the campaign below. In the suite, the Core process replays that committed recording on the same one-hex-line-in, one-JSON-line-out interface. No node runs in CI, and plan §6 #4 holds unchanged: tests replay recordings, and none needs a live `bitcoind`. At Core @ `fc6923c`, `true` tries only the witness-aware reader and `false` only the non-witness one, and each needs full consumption (`src/rpc/rawtransaction.cpp:461-466`, `src/core_io.cpp:154-223`). Never omit the argument: that turns on a heuristic, which `bitcoin-tx` always uses. Core returns `txid`, `hash` (wtxid) and `size`, but no hex, so its bytes are compared by `size` plus `hash`. The baseline is nixpkgs' `bitcoind` 31.1 from the pinned nixpkgs, not `fc6923c`; its transaction deserializer and `DecodeTx` are identical to `fc6923c`'s (docs/btc-verified-integration.md N21). The recording script prints the version, and the recording and README record it. Then the script confirms the one-deserializer behaviour on two regression seeds: a zero-input body with outputs must be accepted with `false` and rejected with `true`, and the `00 00` empty object must be accepted with `true`.
- **Observations compared:** acceptance on each path; re-serialized bytes (ours and btc-verified); Core's `size` and `hash`; txid; wtxid. Error names are not compared.
- **Regression set**, committed and replayed on every run. It holds published legacy and SegWit transactions only, no owner data: the `00 00` empty object; a zero-input body with outputs (non-witness path); a superfluous witness flag (marker and flag with every stack empty); unknown flag bits; truncation at every field; CompactSize boundaries (0xfc/0xfd, 0xffff/0x10000, 2^32 − 1/2^32) and non-canonical CompactSize forms; and a container length of 0x02000001, one over `MAX_SIZE` (0x02000000; Core rejects only lengths above it, `src/serialize.h:359` @ `fc6923c`). Only Core should reject that last case. Its hex is over 64 MiB, beyond Core's 32 MiB HTTP body limit (`src/httpserver.h:82`), so the recording script feeds it to `bitcoin-tx -` on stdin instead (no size limit; `src/bitcoin-tx.cpp:777-789,817-820` at v31.1; send the hex with no trailing newline, which its hex check would reject). `bitcoin-tx` uses the heuristic, but both deserializers reject this case at `ReadCompactSize`'s range check (`src/serialize.h:356` at v31.1), so the recorded rejection is Core's answer on both paths. `bitcoin-tx` comes in the same nixpkgs package.
- **Mutation campaign:** a pinned, seeded mutator over the regression set, with no coverage feedback, so its inputs depend only on the regression set, the seed, the budget and the mutator, never on any of the three implementations. Seed and budget are set at record time, recorded with the recording, and printed in the job log. Keep the budget bounded so the committed recording (inputs plus Core's answers) stays within a few MB.
- **Recording binding:** a digest over the input stream, every recorded Core answer (the over-`MAX_SIZE` rejection included), the mutator version and Core's version. The recording script writes it to a separate committed manifest, never into the recording itself. The suite recomputes the digest from the recording, compares it with the manifest, and fails, naming the stale part, on any mismatch, which forces a re-record. So a hand-edited answer fails the same way as a stale input, and a real re-record changes both files in review. An input with no recorded answer also fails; replay never invents a rejection. A local re-record needs `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-tx` from nix; `lake test` and CI never do.
- **Negative control:** a test-only switch injects one disagreement. The run must then fail, name the input, and print both observations. Without the switch the same input passes.
- **Classification:** every disagreement is matched to a row of `docs/btc-verified-mismatches.md` (Phase 11a, 1 of 2). An unmatched one becomes either a new fix bead (a bug in ours) or a drafted upstream report for btc-verified or Core. Filing a report is outward-facing and needs the owner's go-ahead.
- **CI:** this bead adds the second CI job (the owner's answer to question 3, 2026-10-23). It runs on every PR beside the existing job, outside `lakePackages` and `nix flake check`, as AGENTS.md's named exception says: it fetches Mathlib's prebuilt files (`lake exe cache get`), then builds and tests the btc-verified oracle (`lake build`, `lake test`), runs the no-`sorry` check, the axiom gate and this suite. "CI green" means both jobs pass. It may fetch the pinned btc-verified checkout and the Mathlib cache, but tests never reach the internet once dependencies are fetched. Cap the job's memory.

## Non-goals
- No bridge proofs (Phase 11c).
- No consensus checks (`CheckTransaction`) and no script validation: `bitcoin` has neither.
- Core's transaction-check verdicts, which only libbitcoinkernel offers; question 4's answer did not take that option.
- A fresh campaign on every run, or coverage-guided fuzzing.
- No change to `bitcoin`'s types.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Depends on Phase 11a (1 of 2) (the inventory it classifies against).
- Depends on Phase 11a (2 of 2) (the upgraded copy the btc-verified oracle builds from).
- Depends on the Phase 11 owner-decision bead (all four questions are answered; question 4 fixed the Core oracle as recorded answers).

## Acceptance Criteria
- `Transaction.wtxid` exists, has vectors, and `lake test` passes.
- The regression set and the campaign finish with zero unexplained disagreements. Each explained one cites its inventory row.
- The negative control fails as specified, and passes without the switch.
- The CI job is green and its log records the seed and the budget.
- A deliberately stale recording (one changed input, one edited Core answer, or a changed Core version string) makes the suite fail on the digest check, and an input with no recorded answer fails too. Watch both go red.
- README describes the suite, how to run it, and the expected disagreements.

## Spec refs
plan.md §7 (11b; constraints; the answers to questions 1–4), §6 #4; docs/btc-verified-integration.md N12, N16, N17, N20, N21.

title: Phase 11c (1 of 3): btc-verified bridge package and encoding equivalence
description:
## Outcome
A new Lake package (working name `btc-verified-bridge`; a separate package, per the owner's answer to plan §7 question 3) defines `toVerified` from our transactions to btc-verified's `Tx` and proves that our serializer and btc-verified's encoder produce the same bytes.

## Why this exists
Plan.md §7, deliverable 11c (1 of 3). This is the external analysis's "second deliverable": a machine-checked encoding-equivalence proof, `encode_cyber(t) = encode_verified(convert(t))` for every well-formed `t`. Once it holds, btc-verified's round-trip and canonicality results speak about our serializer's output.

## Scope
- The package requires `bitcoin` by path and btc-verified through our upgraded copy at its pinned commit (Phase 11a, 2 of 2; the owner's answer to plan §7 question 1). It never copies btc-verified's code.
- Licence footing (the owner's answer to plan §7 question 2): the package is "MIT OR Apache-2.0" like every other package, with the dual-licence headers and lakefile licence fields of plan §5. Our upgraded btc-verified copy and Mathlib (both Apache-2.0 only) are pinned build-time dependencies, never copied into the tree.
- `toVerified (tx : Transaction) (w : List (List ByteArray)) (h : tx.WellFormed w) : Tx`, where `Transaction.WellFormed` comes from Phase 4a (3 of 3) (#19; `packages/bitcoin/Bitcoin/TransactionProofs.lean:12-21`). It has nine preconditions: 32-byte txids, sizes < 2^64, `witnesses.length = tx.inputs.size`, and `inputs > 0 ∨ outputs = 0`. It uses the rule our serializer uses:
  - all stacks empty and inputs > 0: `legacy`;
  - all stacks empty with 0 inputs and 0 outputs: `empty`;
  - otherwise `segwit`, bundling input i with stack i. `hWitness` follows from "not all empty".
- Prove, in this order:
  1. outpoint and fixed-width fields (`ByteArray` txid to `Hash256 = Bytes 32`, LE integers);
  2. scripts and counted lists;
  3. per-input witness bundling;
  4. the whole transaction: `(serializeWitnessTransaction tx w).data.toList = encodeTx (toVerified tx w h)`.
- Built and checked in the second CI job (the owner's answer to plan §7 question 3, 2026-10-23), not in `lakePackages` or `nix flake check`: Phase 11b adds that job, and this bead adds the bridge to it. The job fetches Mathlib's prebuilt files (`lake exe cache get`), then runs the bridge's `lake build` and `lake test`, the no-`sorry` check and the axiom gate. AGENTS.md's whole-repo rule names this exception; no other package may leave `lakePackages`. The axiom gate and the no-`sorry` rule apply as in every other package.

## Non-goals
- Parser equivalence (11c, 2 of 3).
- TXID/WTXID (11c, 3 of 3).
- No change to `bitcoin`'s types.
- No Mathlib in `bitcoin` itself; Mathlib reaches only this package, transitively.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Phase 11b: differential evidence first, as the analysis orders it.
- Phase 11a (2 of 2): our upgraded copy of btc-verified on v4.35.0.
- The Phase 11 owner-decision bead. All four of its questions are answered, including the two this bead needs, 2 and 3 (licence footing, package and CI placement).
- Phase 4a (3 of 3) (`Transaction.WellFormed` and the transaction round trip).

## Acceptance Criteria
- The theorem is proven with no hypotheses beyond `WellFormed`. If it needs more, **stop and report**; never prove something weaker.
- `#print axioms` shows only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.
- The second CI job, which builds the package, is green, and so is `nix flake check` ("CI green" means both).
- README lists the theorem and the package's licence footing.

## Spec refs
plan.md §7 (11c 1 of 3; constraints; the answers to questions 1, 2 and 3), §2 (Mathlib only in a separate proofs package); docs/btc-verified-integration.md N5–N7, N13–N15.

title: Phase 11c (2 of 3): parser equivalence with btc-verified on the witness path
description:
## Outcome
The bridge package proves parser equivalence on the witness path. For every byte string, our `parseTransaction bytes` (with `allowWitness := true`) accepts exactly when btc-verified's `decodeTx bytes.toList = some (t, [])`, and then `toVerified` of our parsed value is `t`.

## Why this exists
Plan.md §7, deliverable 11c (2 of 3). The analysis asks for a parser-equivalence theorem, with acceptance and rejection on malformed input treated explicitly. With it, btc-verified's `decodeTx_canonical` describes the bytes our parser accepts.

## Scope
- New lemma on our side: our canonicality. If `parseTransaction bytes = .ok ⟨tx, w⟩`, then `tx.WellFormed w` and `bytes = serializeWitnessTransaction tx w`. Phase 4a (3 of 3) proves only the round trip.
- Direction 1 (ours accepts ⇒ theirs accepts the same value): our canonicality plus 11c (1 of 3) plus `decodeTx_encodeTx`.
- Direction 2 (theirs accepts ⇒ ours accepts): an inverse `ofVerified : Tx → Transaction × List (List ByteArray)` that lands in `WellFormed`, plus `decodeTx_canonical` and our round trip.
- Every acceptance difference listed in `docs/btc-verified-mismatches.md` is excluded by name in the statement, and README lists each exclusion. If a difference shows up that the inventory does not list, add it to the inventory first, with a differential observation.
- The non-witness path (`allowWitness := false`) is out of scope. Its btc-verified counterpart is the `TxBody` codec, not `Tx`, which cannot represent zero-input bodies with outputs (docs/btc-verified-integration.md N17). Record that in README; don't prove anything about it here.

## Non-goals
- Comparing error names.
- TXID/WTXID (11c, 3 of 3).
- Any change to our parser's behaviour. If the proof finds a real bug, file a fix bead.

## Dependencies / ordering
Depends on Phase 11c (1 of 3).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Both directions are proven. Every exclusion matches an inventory row and a Phase 11b observation.
- No weaker statement than this without the owner's approval; **stop and report** instead.
- Axiom gate as in 11c (1 of 3). The CI job that builds the package is green. README is updated.

## Spec refs
plan.md §7 (11c 2 of 3); docs/btc-verified-integration.md N7, N15, N17.

title: Phase 11c (3 of 3): SHA-256 bridge and txid/wtxid agreement with btc-verified
description:
## Outcome
The bridge package proves three things:
- btc-verified's `sha256` equals the FIPS 180-4 specification our `sha256` package is proved against;
- our `txid` and `wtxid` equal btc-verified's `Tx.txid` and `Tx.wtxid` on `toVerified`;
- btc-verified's binding theorems therefore hold for our ids.

## Why this exists
Plan.md §7, deliverable 11c (3 of 3), the analysis's last step ("finally TXID/WTXID relationships"). Carrying `Tx.txid_binding` over to our `txid` needs the two hash functions to agree. btc-verified's SHA-256 is checked only by known-answer tests, so the SHA-256 bridge is a prerequisite here, not only an upstream gift (docs/btc-verified-integration.md N10, N18).

## Scope
- `BtcVerified.Sha256.sha256 m = Spec.sha256_bytes m` for every `m : List UInt8`, where `Spec.sha256_bytes` is lean4-hash's specification (`pure-algebra/lean4-hash` @ `ab7eda4`, MIT; ported in `packages/sha256`), the one `sha256_spec` targets. Then `sha256d` agrees too.
- `(Transaction.txid tx).data.toList = (toVerified tx w h).txid.bytes`, and the same for `wtxid` (added in Phase 11b). Check the byte order: both sides use wire order.
- Carry over `Tx.txid_binding` and `Tx.wtxid_binding` (btc-verified `BtcVerified/Transaction/Txid.lean:65,74`): equal ids imply equal witness-free bodies (or equal transactions), **or** an explicit double-SHA-256 collision. Keep the collision disjunct; never assume collision resistance as an axiom.

## Non-goals
- Sending the SHA-256 bridge upstream. That is Phase 11d and needs the owner's go-ahead; the bridge must carry lean4-hash's MIT notice.
- Any change to the `sha256` package.

## Dependencies / ordering
Depends on Phase 11c (1 of 3). It may run in parallel with 11c (2 of 3).

## Acceptance Criteria
- All three steps are proven, with the axiom gate as in 11c (1 of 3).
- README lists the carried-over binding statements with their collision disjuncts.
- The CI job that builds the package is green.

## Spec refs
plan.md §7 (11c 3 of 3), §1 (SHA-256 row); docs/btc-verified-integration.md N8, N10, N18.

title: Phase 11d: owner decisions on production transaction types and upstream offers
description:
## Outcome
The owner has made two decisions on the evidence from Phase 11a–11c, and both are recorded:
1. **Production types.** Whether to strengthen `bitcoin`'s transaction types: a 32-byte txid type in place of `OutPoint.txid : ByteArray`, and witness stacks bundled per input in place of `WitnessTransaction.witnesses : List (List ByteArray)`. The decision weighs a measured migration cost: the call sites in the PSBT codec, the round-trip theorems in Phase 4a, the bridge proofs, and the app.
2. **Upstream offers.** Which of these to make: the SHA-256 bridge to btc-verified (carrying lean4-hash's MIT notice), mismatch reports drafted in Phase 11b, and whether to offer our toolchain upgrade (Phase 11a, 2 of 2) to btc-verified. The owner's answer to plan §7 question 1 (2026-10-23) authorised no upstream ask, so that last one is a new decision.

## Why this exists
Plan.md §7, deliverable 11d. The analysis says: "Change the production types only when the migration clearly improves the API", and it proposes contributing the proven SHA-256 back. A type change is an API break across every package, and upstream PRs are outward-facing, so both belong to the owner.

## Scope
- Before asking, a work session prepares the evidence: the migration call-site count and the theorems affected, measured on the current `master`; the list of carried-over theorems that would become type-level; and the drafted upstream texts.
- Then present it to the owner. Carry out each decision only after the owner says yes. A type change becomes its own planned bead(s).

## Non-goals
**This bead is deferred and owner-only; no work session may claim it.** No upstream PR or issue is opened without the owner's go-ahead.

## Dependencies / ordering
Depends on Phase 11c (2 of 3) and Phase 11c (3 of 3). It is the last bead of Phase 11.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Each decision is recorded in the close reason or as comments.
- Any upstream links are checked with read-only `gh` calls after the owner acts.

## Spec refs
plan.md §7 (11d); docs/btc-verified-integration.md N13–N18.

title: Phase 1a (2 of 2): secp256k1 C adapter and Lean bindings (parse, verify, recover, sign) with vectors
description:
## Outcome
`packages/secp256k1` is a working Lake package. A small C adapter over nix's libsecp256k1 (0.8.0 at the pinned nixpkgs, recovery module on), linked through Phase 1a (1 of 2)'s target, exposes four operations to Lean:
1. Parse a public key (33-byte compressed or 65-byte uncompressed) and report whether it is valid.
2. ECDSA verify of a 64-byte compact (r‖s) signature, the form Phase 5's capability passes; the matching Wycheproof set is the P1363 file.
3. Recover a public key from a 64-byte compact signature plus a recovery id (0-3) and a 32-byte message hash.
4. Recoverable, deterministic (RFC 6979) signing of a 32-byte hash, returning the 64-byte compact signature and the recovery id.

## Why this exists
- The plan chose crypto path A (owner decision, 2026-10-19). libsecp256k1 does every curve operation behind one small Lean interface, so a verified implementation can replace it after v1.
- Pure packages need these operations as supplied capabilities: the PSBT pubkey check (Phase 4a), and BOLT11 recovery, verification and signing (Phase 5). The app wires them in Phase 7a.

## Scope
- C adapter and Lean `@[extern]` bindings in `packages/secp256k1` only. C lives only in `secp256k1` and `http-curl` (plan §1).
- Switch the `Secp256k1Tests` test driver from a built-only `lean_lib` to a `lean_exe`, so `lake test` actually runs the vectors.
- Document the Lean interface in the package (doc comments plus a README section): signatures, byte layouts, error cases. A replacement implementation must be able to satisfy it.
- Tests decode hex vectors with a small **test-only** hex helper. The library hex codec belongs to Phase 3a (1 of 4); do not add one to `secp256k1`.

## Non-goals
- The link targets and the OpenSSL resolution (Phase 1a, 1 of 2).
- The curl wrapper (Phase 1b). SHA-256 (Phase 2): tests use precomputed 32-byte message hashes, and the Wycheproof digests come from the nix build step below. `secp256k1` gains no Lean dependency (plan §2), and its tests link no OpenSSL for hashing.
- The capability structures that pure packages consume. `bitcoin` and `lightning` define those (Phases 4a and 5); the app fills them (Phase 7a).
- Schnorr/BIP340, key generation, and anything not listed above.
- Entropy for `generate-mnemonic`. Phase 7a decides whether a `getrandom` C call must be added here.

## Critical constraints and failure handling
- Every FFI call returns a Lean-side error value for bad input (wrong length, invalid key, recid out of range, unparsable signature). None may crash the process.
- libsecp256k1's verify accepts only low-S signatures, and the binding does not normalise. A high-S signature is a reject.
- Signing exists only for test vectors in v1. The only private key the tests may use is the BOLT #11 specification's published example key. No other key material is committed.
- **RFC 6979 check first.** Before writing the signing vectors, sign one low-S BOLT #11 example's digest (not the high-S one below) and compare the result with the spec's signature.
- **High-S example, confirmed through the binding first.** The valid example under "Public-key recovery with high-S signature" (`11-payment-encoding.md` L762) is the only one of the 16 valid examples with s > n/2. Before writing the recovery vectors, recover it through this binding (libsecp256k1 does not normalise s) and pin the key it returns. Off-line, with nix libsecp256k1 0.8.0 through a Python binding, it gave `02d0139ce7427d6dfffd26a326c18be754ef1e64672b42694ba5b23ef6e6e7803d`, not the payee key. If the binding returns another key, pin what libsecp256k1 says, use it in this bead's ACs, and note it in README for Phase 5 (1 of 3)'s lookup table. If it differs, the signing acceptance becomes sign → recover → verify for every example instead of byte equality, and README says why.
- **Wycheproof is Apache-2.0 only** (GitHub's licence for C2SP/wycheproof). Committing its JSON would make `secp256k1` "(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND Apache-2.0", the problem Phase 4a (2 of 3) avoids for RIPEMD-160.
  - Take the file through a pinned non-flake input, `inputs.wycheproof = { url = "github:C2SP/wycheproof/7a325932231bd7a724c791c8b0d65ea4d6d2f435"; flake = false; }`, passed to the check derivation and the dev shell (for example through an environment variable the tests read). Commit no Wycheproof file, and no file derived from one.
  - **Digests.** Wycheproof ECDSA entries carry `msg`, not its hash, and libsecp256k1 exports no plain SHA-256. Compute the digests in a nix build step: a `runCommand` derivation runs python3's `hashlib.sha256` over each `msg` of the pinned input's JSON and writes `tcId digest` lines. Pass its output path to the check derivation **and** the dev shell, so host-side `lake test` reads it too. Commit no derived file.
  - If that cannot work, stop and report, and raise a deferred `owner-decision` bead.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Depends on Phase 1a (1 of 2): the link target and the OpenSSL resolution.
- Phase 1b and Phase 7a wait for both Phase 1a beads.

## Acceptance Criteria
- **Recovery vectors.** For each BOLT #11 specification example (`11-payment-encoding.md` at lightning/bolts @ `191462825ae341f0a27098765c075f01ca9bc6c2`), recover the published payee key `03e7156ae33b0a208d0744199163177e909e80176e55d97a2f221ede0f934dd9ad` from its 65-byte signature, for the 15 low-S examples. The high-S example (L762, no `n` field) recovers, without normalising, to the key pinned above (`02d0139c…` unless the binding said otherwise), and the test asserts that pinned key. Hash the signing preimage (SHA-256 over the lower-cased hrp bytes plus the data part; the all-upper-case example at L704 carries the same signature as L683's invoice) ahead of time, with a committed generator script that uses a nix-provided tool, and check in the resulting 32-byte digests. The vector file's provenance line names BOLT #11 @ `1914628`, `11-payment-encoding.md`, CC-BY-4.0, "extracted and reformatted".
- **Signing vectors.** Sign each precomputed digest with the spec's published example private key. For every example except L762, the compact signature and recid equal the spec's; or, if the RFC 6979 check above failed, each signature recovers the payee key and verifies. For L762, libsecp256k1 signs low-S: our signature is (r, n − s_spec) with the same recid 1 (checked off-line), and it recovers `03e7156…`.
- **Verify vectors.** Wycheproof ECDSA secp256k1 vectors from the flake input above, with digests from the nix build step.
  - Use the P1363 `r||s` file, `testvectors_v1/ecdsa_secp256k1_sha256_p1363_test.json`, which matches the compact signature verify takes.
  - State the counts, including invalid cases rejected. Where the file marks a high-S signature valid, count it as an expected reject and say so in README.
  - Expected, from the file and to be confirmed through the binding: 252 tests, 95 accepted, 157 rejected (85 invalid, of which 18 have a non-64-byte signature, plus 72 "valid" high-S). Every public key is 65 bytes, uncompressed.
- **Negative tests.** A tampered signature fails verify; a wrong-length or off-curve key is rejected; recid 4 is rejected. Watch each go red against a deliberately broken binding first (AGENTS.md: a test that never failed proves nothing).
### Common definition of done (plan §4, every work session)
- `nix build` and `nix flake check` exit 0. The flake check runs `lake build && lake test` for every package listed in `lakePackages` in `flake.nix`, inside the nix sandbox, then runs the app. Stage new files (`git add`) before running `nix flake check`: a flake sees only tracked files.
- In each touched package, `nix develop -c lake build` and `nix develop -c lake test` exit 0.
- No `sorry`: `grep -rnw sorry --include='*.lean' --exclude-dir=.lake packages` prints nothing (CI runs the same check from Phase 2 on).
- `#print axioms` on every theorem this bead lists shows only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Each listed theorem is added to the package's committed axiom-gate test (Phase 2's pattern); `lake test` fails on any axiom outside the three. The gate is an allowlist of those three and contains no "sorry" substring. No `native_decide` in library or proof modules; test files may use it.
- The vector counts this bead states pass. Each test asserts that the number of vectors it loaded equals a pinned constant, so a dropped vector fails, and the test output prints each count (for example `<set> valid: N/N`).
- `README.md` is updated: what the package now provides, vector sources and counts, and anything this bead says to document.
- `AGENTS.md` rules hold, including "Reference only" for any value taken from cyberkrill. New Lean, C and script files we write carry the dual-licence header; third-party and copied files follow the rule below, and JSON and other formats without comments need none.
- **Safety.** Tests use only published vectors, published test mnemonics, the BOLT #11 specification's published example private key (tests only), recordings from a throwaway regtest node, and synthetic or script-generated fixtures under the third-party rule (for example cyberkrill's captured outputs on those inputs, synthetic provider responses, our own LNURL and LUD JSON, values a committed script derives from published inputs). Never anything from the owner's node, wallets or devices. Tests never reach the internet, port 8332 or `~/.bitcoin`. Nothing committed contains private keys, seeds, xprvs, tprvs or WIF keys, or real addresses, xpubs or device dumps, apart from that BOLT #11 example key. No hardware wallets, no signing outside test vectors, no broadcast, no mainnet funds.

description:

The curl wrapper is not written yet. Calling something trivial is enough, such as `curl_version()` and creating a libsecp256k1 context.

## Why this exists

title: Phase 1b (1 of 2): http-curl package (C wrapper over libcurl plus a Lean interface)
description:
## Outcome
`packages/http-curl` provides HTTPS and HTTP requests to Lean:
- a ~100-line C wrapper over nix libcurl (OpenSSL backend);
- a small Lean interface with GET and POST, request headers, HTTP basic auth, a bounded response size, connect and total timeouts, and structured errors;
- a working CA bundle on any Linux host.

## Why this exists
Owner decision (2026-10-18): Lean 4.35 has no HTTP client in core, so we write our own thin libcurl wrapper. Its Lean interface is small enough for Lean core's own client to replace it later. Every network command in v1 goes through it:
- Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC: plain HTTP to localhost with basic auth (Phase 8);
- price feeds, LNURL-pay and Fedimint config fetch over HTTPS (Phase 9).

Phase 1b is split in two to keep each work session small: this wrapper, its CA logic and their tests on a minimal localhost responder, then the reusable recording stub server (2 of 2).

## Scope
- C wrapper and Lean bindings in `packages/http-curl`. The libcurl link target from Phase 1a's spike lives here.
- The Lean API covers:
  - method GET or POST, URL, a header list, an optional body, optional basic-auth user and password;
  - a maximum response size, a connect timeout and a total timeout.
  - The result is the status code, the response headers (or at least content type), and the body bytes, or a structured error.
- Error kinds at least: DNS/connect failure, timeout, TLS/certificate failure, response larger than the limit, and other curl errors carrying their curl code and message.
  - An HTTP status of 4xx/5xx is a normal result, not an error. Callers decide.
- **CA fix.** A nix-built binary otherwise finds no CA bundle on non-NixOS hosts.
  - Lean 4.35 core has no CA-path list to reuse. Probe a fixed list of common bundle paths (for example `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`, `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt`, `/etc/ssl/cert.pem`), listed in README. Do not embed nix's cacert bundle: plan §2 allows either, and the probe list is the one chosen, so the binary carries no MPL-2.0 data (`pkgs.cacert`'s `meta.license.spdxId` at the pinned nixpkgs) and Phase 10a (2 of 3)'s empty-root run exercises the probe path.
  - Always honour `SSL_CERT_FILE` when it is set. The wrapper reads `SSL_CERT_FILE` on each request, not once at start-up.
  - When `SSL_CERT_FILE` is unset or empty, no test hook is set and no probe path exists, the wrapper returns the certificate error without sending a request, so it never falls through to curl's `--with-ca-fallback`.
  - A test-only hook replaces the fallback, so tests can exercise it without touching the host's bundle. The hook is a field of the Lean request config (for example `caFallback : Option System.FilePath`), set only by tests; no environment variable, so the release binary has none.
  - The wrapper always sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO` itself: `SSL_CERT_FILE` if set and non-empty, else the fallback (the test hook's path when set, otherwise the first existing probe path). It never relies on OpenSSL's default verify paths.
  - Why: the pinned nixpkgs' `setup.sh` (`pkgs/stdenv/generic/setup.sh:1004-1009`) exports `NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE=/no-cert-file.crt` and `SSL_CERT_FILE=/no-cert-file.crt` unless `IN_NIX_SHELL` is `impure`, so in the check sandbox `SSL_CERT_FILE` is never unset by default. nixpkgs OpenSSL carries `nix-ssl-cert-file.patch`, curl is built with `--with-ca-fallback` (`curlMinimal/package.nix:199`), and the toolchain's static OpenSSL is unpatched.
  - Each CA case runs in a child process whose environment sets or removes **both** `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE` explicitly (`IO.Process.spawn` env entries with `none` remove a variable). Run the CA tests both in `nix develop` and in `nix flake check`.
- **A minimal localhost responder for these tests**, over plain HTTP and over TLS with a self-signed certificate: it echoes a body and headers, answers a 401 to wrong basic-auth credentials, sends an oversized body, and stalls. title: Phase 3a (4 of 4): scriptPubKey to address and back (P2PKH, P2SH, P2WPKH, P2WSH, P2TR) per network
description:
## Outcome
`packages/bitcoin` converts between a scriptPubKey and its address string for P2PKH, P2SH, P2WPKH, P2WSH and P2TR, on each network cyberkrill supports. Per-type round-trip theorems are proven, BIP350's segwit address vectors and BIP173's v0 ones pass, and BIP173's three bech32 v1+ addresses are rejected. This bead completes Phase 3a.

## Why this exists
Every app command that prints or accepts an address goes through this:
- `onchain-decode-psbt` outputs;
- the UTXO listing;
- PSBT outputs;
- BOLT11 fallback addresses.

- A network type covering mainnet, testnet, signet and regtest. Check cyberkrill's `Network` usage for exactly which networks it accepts.

  - P2SH 0x05 on mainnet, 0xc4 otherwise.
- Segwit hrps: `bc`, `tb` (testnet and signet), `bcrt`.
- Witness rules (BIP141/BIP350):
  - v0 programs are 20 or 32 bytes, encoded with bech32;
  - v1+ programs are 2-40 bytes, encoded with bech32m.
  - The BIP350 valid vectors include unknown witness versions up to 16, so handle generic witness programs for those vectors, not only P2TR.
- Script templates: P2PKH, P2SH, `OP_0 <20>`, `OP_0 <32>`, `OP_1 <32>`, and generic `OP_n <program>`.

## Non-goals
- Descriptors. Bitcoin Core handles them through RPC in Phase 8.
- Address derivation from public keys (no hash160 here).

## Critical constraints and failure handling
- Decoding an address checks it against the expected network and reports a mismatch distinctly.
- The bech32 layer is called with the 90-character limit.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Depends on Phase 3a (1 of 4) for hex, Phase 3a (2 of 4) for Base58Check, and Phase 3a (3 of 4) for bech32/m.
- With those three, this bead completes Phase 3a, which Phases 3b, 4a-4d, 5 and 6 wait for.

Theorems, with `#print axioms`:

It is false on raw strings: BIP173 L306 and BIP350 L186 are upper case, and encoding returns lower case.

title: Phase 3a (2 of 4): base58 and Base58Check codecs with proofs
description:
## Outcome
`packages/bitcoin` gains our own base58 encoder and decoder, using the Bitcoin alphabet and keeping leading zero bytes as leading `1`s. It also gains Base58Check: payload plus a 4-byte SHA-256d checksum. Both carry proofs.

## Why this exists
Base58Check is needed by P2PKH/P2SH addresses (Phase 3a, 4 of 4), SLIP-132 (Phase 4c) and BOLT11 fallback addresses (Phase 5).

## Scope
- `base58Encode : ByteArray → String` and `base58Decode : String → Option ByteArray` (or `Except`), with leading zeros handled.
- `base58CheckEncode` and `base58CheckDecode`, the latter verifying the checksum with `sha256d` from `packages/sha256`.
- Import **only** `rawVectors` from lean-miniscript @ `cb9bc5f`, `KeyEncodingExamples.lean` L29-50: 21 vectors taken from Bitcoin Core's `base58_encode_decode.json` @ `9be056a` (pinned at L21-23). Its two `native_decide` checks (L52-55) become `lake test` assertions.
  - Copy no WIF vectors (`wifVectors`, L57) and nothing from `BIP32Examples.lean` (it holds xprv/tprv strings).
  - Do not import `invalidCoreKeys` (L87): its 70 strings come from Core's `key_io_invalid.json`, upstream checks them with `decodeWIF` (L159-160), and most are valid base58. The invalid cases are our own:
    - `base58Decode` rejects each of `0`, `O`, `I`, `l`, a space and one non-ASCII character (6 cases);

- Address logic (Phase 3a, 4 of 4).
- Any error-detection guarantee for Base58Check. It has none, so none is claimed (plan §2).

## Critical constraints and failure handling
- The decoder rejects characters outside the alphabet (`0`, `O`, `I`, `l`) and never panics.
- Base58Check decode fails on a short input (under 4 bytes) and on a checksum mismatch, with distinguishable errors.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Depends on Phase 2 (`sha256d`) and Phase 3a (1 of 4), because the vectors are hex.
- Phase 3a (4 of 4) waits for this bead.

- **Base58:**
  - `base58Decode (base58Encode b) = some b` for every byte array, including leading zeros;
  - `base58Decode s = some b → base58Encode b = s`.
- **Base58Check:**
  - round-trip;
  - **soundness:** decode succeeds only when the 4-byte SHA-256d checksum matches.

- the 21 `rawVectors`, and our own invalid cases: 6 bad characters and 2 Base58Check rejections (print each count);

- invalid characters;

    - hrp characters outside 33-126;
    - a missing separator;
    - characters outside the charset;
    - an empty hrp;
    - checksums under 6 characters;
    - a wrong checksum;
    - a string over the caller's length limit.

title: Phase 3a (1 of 4): bitcoin primitives: hex, CompactSize, exact msat Amount
description:
## Outcome
`packages/bitcoin` gains three codecs:
- **hex** encode and decode;
- **CompactSize** encode and decode, rejecting non-canonical encodings;
- an exact **`Amount`** type held in millisatoshis, with BTC, sats and msats parsing and printing that never uses floating point.

Their round-trip and exactness theorems are proven.

## Why this exists
Every later `bitcoin`, `lightning` and app bead builds on these:
- CompactSize frames transactions and PSBTs.
- `Amount` replaces cyberkrill's `f64` BTC arithmetic. That is a deliberate improvement (plan §3, "Exact amounts vs f64"): the port parses Core's JSON numbers exactly and uses msat `Amount` throughout.

Phase 3a is split into four beads to keep each work session small. This one has no dependency on the other three.

## Scope
- `hex`: lower-case output; decoding accepts upper and lower case and rejects odd length and non-hex characters.
- `CompactSize`: encode and decode Bitcoin's variable-length integer (1, 3, 5 or 9 bytes).
  - Decoding rejects a non-canonical encoding: a value encoded in more bytes than it needs.
  - Decoding reports truncated input.
- `Amount` in msat, with:
  - constructors and accessors for BTC, sats and msats;
  - parse and print of decimal BTC (up to 11 fractional digits, since 1 msat = 1e-11 BTC), sats (up to 3 fractional digits) and integer msats;
  - rejection of sub-msat precision.
  - Also convert an exact decimal (mantissa, decimal exponent), the form `Lean.JsonNumber` keeps, to `Amount`. Phase 8 parses Core's JSON amounts this way, and sub-msat precision is rejected there too.
  - Decide and document whether negative amounts and amounts above 21 million BTC are representable.
- **CLI amount grammar.** A parser for the grammar cyberkrill's CLI accepts, `AmountInput::from_str` (`cyberkrill-core/src/bitcoin_rpc.rs:219-283`), which Phase 7a and later commands use:
  - trim and lower-case the input; an empty string is an error;
  - suffixes in this order: `msats`/`msat` (an integer), then `sats`/`sat`, then `btc`, then a bare number, which is **BTC**;
  - cyberkrill parses sats and BTC through `f64` and rounds to the nearest msat (`:86`, `:122`), so it accepts `0.000000000001` (→ 0 msat), exponent forms (`1e-3`) and Rust's `inf`/`nan` spellings. The port rejects sub-msat precision (plan §2), exponent forms and `inf`/`nan`. Phase 7a lists these under README "Deltas taken" and tests each by name.
  - Rust's `f64` and `u64` `FromStr` grammars (from Rust's documentation; not run against cyberkrill) also accept `.5`, `5.`, a leading `+` (`+5msat`, `+0.5btc`), `infinity` and `-0`. Name each one as accepted or rejected, test each by name, and list every rejection under README "Deltas taken" (create that section if it is missing; Phase 7a extends it).
- Switch the `BitcoinTests` driver from a built-only `lean_lib` to a `lean_exe`, so `lake test` runs the vectors.

## Non-goals
- Transaction and PSBT serialization (Phase 4a, copied from lean-miniscript).
- Fiat conversion (Phase 9a).

## Critical constraints and failure handling
- **Overlap with Phase 4a.** lean-miniscript @ `cb9bc5f` has its own `compactSize` in `LeanMiniscript/Bitcoin/Serialization.lean`, and a decoder with proofs in `Deserialization.lean` and `DeserializationProofs.lean`. Phase 4a (1 of 3) copies those files.
  - Take that code under the copy rules (provenance comment, MIT notice beside it), unless a reason to write our own is recorded in README. `Deserialization.lean` imports `LegacySighash` and through it `LeanHash160`, the chain Phase 4a (1 of 3) cuts, so copy slices into one module: `Bitcoin/Serialization.lean` whole (it imports only `Lean`), `Deserialization.lean` L11-79 (`DecodeError` … `decodeAll`: no tx types, no hashing) and the matching `DeserializationProofs.lean` lemmas L7-179 (`unsignedLE_length` … `readCompactSize_ok`, which ends before `readByteVector_ok` at L180). The slices use nothing outside themselves except the namespace header. The provenance comment names the line ranges, and Phase 4a (1 of 3) imports this module and copies only the remaining lines.
  - Upstream's `readCompactSize` already rejects non-minimal encodings (`Deserialization.lean:33-45`, `.nonCanonicalCompactSize`), and its round-trip `readCompactSize_compactSize` and `readCompactSize_ok` (accepted bytes are `compactSize value ++ rest`, which gives canonicity) are proven (`DeserializationProofs.lean:31`, `:117`).
  - Phase 4a (1 of 3) owns the final reconcile: `bitcoin` must end Phase 4a with a single CompactSize codec, and README says which one is canonical.
- Parsers return errors and never panic.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Plan §4: Phase 3a depends on Phase 2, so this bead does too (even though these three codecs don't hash).
- Phase 3a (2 of 4) waits for this bead (the base58 vectors are hex), and so does Phase 3a (4 of 4, address ↔ script).
- Phase 3b, every Phase 4 bead, Phase 5 and Phase 6 wait for all four Phase 3a beads.

The bound is the wire format's: upstream's `readCompactSize_compactSize` takes `bound : value < 2 ^ 64` (`DeserializationProofs.lean:31`), because `compactSize` writes only 8 bytes (`0xff :: unsignedLE 8 value`, `Serialization.lean:16`).

  - sub-msat precision rejected.

- hex vectors, including odd length and bad characters;

title: Phase 3b (2 of 2): bech32/bech32m 4-error detection theorem, per variant (data part of at most 89 characters)
description:
## Outcome
A proven theorem, in `bitcoin`, or, if the proof needs Mathlib, in a new `bitcoin-proofs` package (plan §6 #2). It states, **per variant**, as BIP173 "Checksum" and BIP350 claim it: for a string valid under variant v (bech32 or bech32m) whose data part is **at most 89 characters**, **any substitution of 1 to 4 data characters yields a string that variant v's checksum verification rejects**.

## Why this exists
This is the headline checksum guarantee at proof level M: checksums catch the errors their specification says they catch. Addresses are at most 90 characters, so the guarantee covers every address the port handles.

## Scope
- Follow the proof plan that Phase 3b (1 of 2) committed. Read its verdict first.
- State the theorem over Phase 3a (3 of 4)'s exact `polymod` and decoder. Do not prove it about a separate model unless the model is proven equal to the code.
- "Data characters" means every character after the separator, checksum included (BIP173's "data part"). A substitution replaces a data character by another bech32 charset character, so the hrp, the separator position and the case are unchanged.
- The statement in Lean: for each variant `v`, every hrp `h`, and all data vectors `d`, `d'` with `∀ x ∈ d ++ d', x < 32` (or Phase 3a (3 of 4)'s 5-bit element type, such as `Fin 32`), of equal length with `6 ≤ d.length ≤ 89` (the data part including its 6 checksum symbols): if `verifyChecksum v h d = true` and `d` and `d'` differ in at least 1 and at most 4 positions, then `verifyChecksum v h d' = false`.
- Corollary over the real decoder: if `s`'s data part has at most 89 characters (in particular, any `s` that `decode` accepts with the address limit 90) and `s` decodes with variant `v`, and `t` differs from `s` in 1 to 4 data-part positions, each replaced by a charset character, then `decode t` (with the same limit) does not return variant `v`. In Lean, the 1-4 positions are those where the charset index of `toLower t[i]` differs from that of `toLower s[i]`, and `t` agrees with `s` at every other position. A character-level reading is false: `019PYQ3G7` and `019pyq3g7` are both valid bech32 and differ in 4 positions, each by a charset character.
- Both bounds are needed, and neither is a weakening. Without the length bound the corollary is false: `a1gys8lu7cdxlpcmqu3wx5pppqcdmpwulwkwwajp6xtj84mvnjlez70e6thh9ux2ehlp7zne22wqvwekka3qcgxcsphe` and `a1hys8lu7cdxtpcmqu3wx5pppqcdmpwulwkwwajp6xtj84mvnjlez70e6thh9ux2ehlp7zne22wqv0ekka3qcgxcsphn` (92 characters, data part 90) are both valid bech32, 4 substitutions apart, and `a1dmr7hv6lk6kq4apwtt9szy9puq3038tkjy22s23ja5l78pnc46vsxsdmpwpefz2umwuwpe5mrngdrnyynn26xapf2c` / `a1jmr7hv6lk6zq4apwtt9szy9puq3038tkjy22s23ja5l78pnc46vsxsdmpwpefz2umwuwpe5mrngvrnyynn26xapf2j` are a bech32m pair. Without `x < 32` it is false at 2 positions: `a12uel5l` has data `[10,28,25,31,20,31]`, and `[10,28,24,63,20,31]` gives the same `polymod`.
- Cover both variants (bech32 and bech32m). `polymod`'s linear part is shared by both, so one finite fact can cover the two (Phase 3b (1 of 2)'s plan).
- This per-variant statement corrects a false earlier wording ("any substitution of at most 4 data characters is rejected by the decoder", across both variants); it is a correction, not a weakening, and plan §2 states it the same way.
- Only if Phase 3b (1 of 2)'s plan needs Mathlib: create `packages/bitcoin-proofs`, which requires `bitcoin` plus Mathlib through a pinned flake input (the sandbox cannot fetch it). Add it to `lakePackages` in `flake.nix`. Its lakefile carries `license := "MIT OR Apache-2.0"` and `licenseFiles := #["../../LICENSE-MIT", "../../LICENSE-APACHE"]`, like the other seven. Keep `bitcoin` itself Mathlib-free (plan §2). Update AGENTS.md's package count, README's package table and plan §2's diagram to include it.

## Non-goals
- BOLT11, LNURL and invites. They exceed 90 characters, so they only get round-trip and checksum soundness (plan §6 default #2).
- Burst errors, insertions and deletions. They are not part of the statement.
- **Cross-variant acceptance** is not covered, and is false: 4 substitutions turn the valid bech32 string `bc1qw508d6qejxtdg4y5r3zarvary0c5xw7kv8f3t4` (BIP173's P2WPKH example) into the valid bech32m string `bc1qw508d6qejxtdg4y5r3zarvary0c5uw7ka8f3x3` (indices 32, 36, 40, 41).
- **The segwit address decoder's witness-version rules** are not covered: changing the version character `q`→`p` plus 3 more substitutions gives `bc1pw508s6qejrtdg4y5r3zarvary0c5xwykv8f3t4`, a valid bech32m string that BIP350's reference `decode("bc", …)` accepts as witness version 1 with a 20-byte program.
- Substituting `1` (it moves the separator, since BIP173 takes the last `1`) and case-only changes (accepted, same value) are not substitutions in the statement's sense.

## Critical constraints and failure handling
- **Stop and report, never weaken.** If the theorem proves out of reach, follow the common stop mechanics with what was tried and where it stuck (owner decision, 2026-10-19). Do not prove a weaker statement than the one above without the owner's approval, for example fewer errors, data parts shorter than 89 characters, only one of the two variants, or a model instead of the code.
- No `native_decide` in the proof (plan §6 default #3). Kernel `decide` over a finite search is allowed if the theorem adds at most 10 minutes to `nix flake check`.
- A `bitcoin-proofs` package must still pass `nix flake check` in the sandbox. Mathlib's build time there counts against the 10 minutes: measure it and report it. Stop and report only if Mathlib makes `nix flake check` exceed that budget, or is otherwise infeasible.

## Dependencies / ordering
- Depends on Phase 3b (1 of 2), and through it on all four Phase 3a beads.
- Nothing in v1 is blocked by it except Phase 10's release beads.
- If the owner drops or re-scopes the theorem, close or re-scope this bead. Otherwise Phase 10a (1 of 3) and Phase 10a (3 of 3) never unblock.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The theorem is stated as above, and `#print axioms` on it shows only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.
- README quotes BIP173's wording, the per-variant theorem, the two Non-goal counterexamples and why the corollary's length bound and the `x < 32` hypothesis are needed.
- The work-session report shows the theorem's exact statement and the measured time it adds to `nix flake check`.
### Common definition of done (plan §4, every work session)
- `nix build` and `nix flake check` exit 0. The flake check runs `lake build && lake test` for every package listed in `lakePackages` in `flake.nix`, inside the nix sandbox, then runs the app. Stage new files (`git add`) before running `nix flake check`: a flake sees only tracked files.
- In each touched package, `nix develop -c lake build` and `nix develop -c lake test` exit 0.
- No `sorry`: `grep -rnw sorry --include='*.lean' --exclude-dir=.lake packages` prints nothing (CI runs the same check from Phase 2 on).
- `#print axioms` on every theorem this bead lists shows only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Each listed theorem is added to the package's committed axiom-gate test (Phase 2's pattern); `lake test` fails on any axiom outside the three. The gate is an allowlist of those three and contains no "sorry" substring. No `native_decide` in library or proof modules; test files may use it.
- The vector counts this bead states pass. Each test asserts that the number of vectors it loaded equals a pinned constant, so a dropped vector fails, and the test output prints each count (for example `<set> valid: N/N`).
- `README.md` is updated: what the package now provides, vector sources and counts, and anything this bead says to document.
- `AGENTS.md` rules hold, including "Reference only" for any value taken from cyberkrill. New Lean, C and script files we write carry the dual-licence header; third-party and copied files follow the rule below, and JSON and other formats without comments need none.
- **Safety.** Tests use only published vectors, published test mnemonics, the BOLT #11 specification's published example private key (tests only), recordings from a throwaway regtest node, and synthetic or script-generated fixtures under the third-party rule (for example cyberkrill's captured outputs on those inputs, synthetic provider responses, our own LNURL and LUD JSON, values a committed script derives from published inputs). Never anything from the owner's node, wallets or devices. Tests never reach the internet, port 8332 or `~/.bitcoin`. Nothing committed contains private keys, seeds, xprvs, tprvs or WIF keys, or real addresses, xpubs or device dumps, apart from that BOLT #11 example key. No hardware wallets, no signing outside test vectors, no broadcast, no mainnet funds.
- **Third-party material** (`AGENTS.md` "Licence", plan §5):
  - Admitted in the tree, each with a provenance sidecar or header line (source URL, commit, path, licence), never the dual-licence header: MIT, BSD, ISC, CC0 or public domain, and CC-BY-4.0 (attribution and a note of any changes, for example "extracted and reformatted", kept in the sidecar). Material offered under a choice that includes MIT (such as fedimint-lite's `MIT OR Apache-2.0`) is taken under MIT.
  - Kept out of the tree: Apache-2.0-only, share-alike (CC-BY-SA) and unlicensed material. Use a pinned non-flake input read at test time, or replace it with vectors we generate ourselves.
  - Copied code whose upstream file has no header gets a provenance comment (upstream repo, commit, path, "MIT") with the upstream MIT notice in a file beside it, never the dual-licence header.
  - In a Lean file the provenance line is the first line and a `--` line comment (or `/- … -/`), never a `/-! … -/` doc comment, for example `-- Copied from <repo> @ <commit>, <path>; MIT, see <notice file>`. JSON and other formats without comments get the sidecar.
- **Stop mechanics.** If this bead says stop and report: commit no weakened statement, `br defer` the bead, add label `owner-decision`, comment what was tried (`br comments add`), and end the work session blocked.
- **Follow-ups.** A delta or stricter check you think v1 needs goes in a new bead created deferred with label `owner-decision`, and in README "Deltas not taken". Never implement it unranked.
- **Upstream fixes.** A fix that would also help upstream (lean4-hash, lean-miniscript) goes in the committed `docs/upstream-fixes.md` (file, problem, fix), not in a br comment. Phase 10a (3 of 3) turns that file into patches.

## Spec refs
plan.md §2 (`bitcoin` row, bech32/m obligations), §4 (Phase 3b row), §6 default #2 (proof scope, Mathlib to `bitcoin-proofs`, back to the owner if out of reach). BIP173 "Checksum" section, BIP350.

## Why this exists
The theorem is the headline checksum guarantee at proof level M, and the riskiest proof in v1:
- BIP173's bound for data parts of up to 89 characters most likely comes from a computer search, not a short argument;
- a kernel `decide` over that search space may be infeasible;
- if the proof needs Mathlib, plan §6 #2 puts it in a new `bitcoin-proofs` package. Mathlib cannot be fetched inside the nix sandbox, so it would come in as a pinned flake input, the package would be listed in `lakePackages`, and the sorry grep keeps `--exclude-dir=.lake`. Mathlib's build time in the sandbox then counts against the budget below.
